newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW-Bank of Ireland sees more growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Bank of Ireland sees more growth.

text.p: Bank of Ireland Plc, one of the Republic of Ireland's largest financial groups, on Wednesday announced an 8.8 percent rise in annual profits and said the bank was looking for further growth this year.

"The outlook and conditions in all the markets in which we are operating are good...here, the United States, everywhere. Pressure on margins continues but we will continue to see good performance and good volume growth," chief executive Pat Molloy said in a telephone interview.
The bank raised pretax profits in the year to end-March 1997 to 395.6 million Irish pounds from 363.7 million a year earlier.
The results and a proposed total dividend of 17.75p per share, up from 15.25p a year earlier, were broadly in line with analysts' expectations.
"We haven't produced any surprises. The Irish economy continues to perform very well and the outlook is good. It's a good time to be in the banking business," Molloy said.

Molloy said the bank had grown across the board, adding that growth was strong in Northern Ireland, Britain and the Republic of Ireland. Its retail division raised pre-tax profits by 11.8 percent to 204.4 million Irish pounds, with lending up 12 percent. The bank said it held 20 percent of the market for new Irish mortgages.
Molloy said his bank's strong performance and the healthy economy meant provisions remained modest at 20 million Irish pounds, down slightly from the previous year.

"Provisions reflect the times in which we are living. The economy is strong...and the quality of our loan book is very good. For the last three years we have been building up our non-designated specific provision, which is a further element of conservatism (in our accounting)," he said.

Analysts have also described the bank's dividend policy, with cover almost as high as three times earnings, as cautious compared with other sector players. The bank last year bought Britain's Bristol & West, one of the country's top 10 building societies for 600 million stg cash and analysts expected the bank to focus on rebuilding capital.

"We had a large flood of capital (to pay for Bristol & West) but we believe in a progressive dividend policy. We think cover of three times is a bit too strong but we are producing a pretty good dividend increase of 16 percent," he said.
Molloy said the bank's firepower had been dented "a little" by the Bristol & West acquisition but said Bank of Ireland continued to "look around". He declined to give details.
